title: Why You Must Make The Complex Simple
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin observes that many teachers unintentionally overcomplicate lessons, leaving even strong students confused, disengaged, and misbehaving, and that teachers often misdiagnose the resulting poor work as low ability and respond by dumbing down content rather than fixing their delivery. He offers six universal fixes: talking less and getting to the point, pausing often to let understanding land, focusing on a single objective, adding vivid concrete details, modeling as if performing the task themselves, and returning always to the single objective rather than diluting it. He frames disciplined, purposeful speech as the core skill, arguing that when teachers master it, students are steadily exposed to more challenging material and can advance well beyond peers in less disciplined classrooms.
points: Many teachers unintentionally overcomplicate lessons, producing confusion that gets misdiagnosed as low student ability.
The common but wrong fix is dumbing down content rather than correcting the teacher's delivery.
Six specific fixes are offered: talk less, pause often, focus on one objective, add vivid details, model precisely, and stick to one objective.
Disciplined, purposeful speech is framed as the core skill that separates good and struggling teaching.
Mastering this skill lets students handle steadily more challenging material and outpace peers in less disciplined classrooms.
quotes: A problem with education today is that many (many) teachers make their lessons too complex.
Again and again, I observe teachers taking basic concepts and twisting them into medieval labyrinths that leave even the sharpest students scratching their heads.
Noticing this, as well as the shoddy work produced, the teacher assumes it’s because their class is low academically.
Most teachers talk too much. They use many words to describe what can be better understood with a few. Be brief, clear, direct, then zip it.
Bad teaching is when a teacher opens their mouth without clear purpose. Yes, random thoughts might be tangentially related, but you’re not talking with a friend.
You must be hyper-concentrated on your objective and driven to 100 percent understanding. In this way, academic growth and progression are inevitable.
